faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Brooklyn?
faqs.a: Cost depends on what is in the house, how long it has been there, and how many openings need to be sealed. We start with an inspection and a written quote, and we do not promise prices over the phone before we have seen the entries.

faqs.q: When do animals get into Brooklyn attics most often?
faqs.a: Our crew's Brooklyn work centers on Norway rats in basements and restaurant blocks, pigeons on cornices and signs, and raccoons working the Prospect Park edge. The pattern follows the housing and the habitat: east river and prospect park keeps animals close, and once one finds a way into a roofline, chimney, or crawlspace here, it usually comes back until every entry is sealed. That is why we pair removal with proofing on every Brooklyn job rather than just taking the animal out.

Brooklyn.housing_era: Brooklyn is brownstones and limestone rowhouses in Park Slope and Bedford-Stuyvesant, pre-war elevator apartments across Flatbush and Bay Ridge, converted industrial lofts in Williamsburg and Bushwick, and postwar attached homes out toward Canarsie and Mill Basin. Shared walls, old cornices, and aging flat roofs give rats, pigeons, and squirrels endless routes between buildings.

Brooklyn.wildlife_intro:
Brooklyn keeps our crew busy with Norway rats in basements and restaurant blocks, pigeons on cornices and signs, and raccoons working the Prospect Park edge. East River and Prospect Park  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Brooklyn. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Brooklyn jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.
